summary: Defines a new option for the PIM Hello message that lets a router announce an identifier for one of its interfaces. Neighbors can then use that identifier to tell exactly which interface of the router they are talking about, which helps other PIM protocols. It is a standards-track extension.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers say hello to their neighbors. This adds a name tag for each doorway on the router, so neighbors can say exactly which door they mean.

subtitle: A PIM Hello option that lets a router tag each of its interfaces with a 64-bit identifier its neighbors can refer to.

tldr.problem: PIM protocols sometimes need to refer to one particular interface of a neighboring router, but interfaces can be unnumbered or have only IPv6 link-local addresses, which are poor identifiers.
tldr.mechanism: A new PIM Hello option, type 31, carries an 8-byte Interface Identifier made of a 32-bit Router Identifier and a 32-bit Local Interface Identifier.
tldr.outcome: Other PIM protocols, such as PIM over Reliable Transport, can use the identifier to say which interface a message belongs to. How it is used is left to those protocols.

today: RFC 6395 is a Proposed Standard from October 2011. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Interfaces Need Identifiers
sections.content:
This document defines a new option for PIM Hello messages (RFC 4601) that carries an Interface Identifier. A router generates an identifier for each of its PIM-enabled interfaces so that every interface has a different one. The identifiers can optionally be made unique within a wider scope, for example an administrative domain.

The RFC gives one example of use: PIM over Reliable Transport (PORT), where a single transport connection is used between two routers that have several interfaces connecting them. If those interfaces are unnumbered or use IPv6 link-local addresses, the identifier in a PORT Join/Prune message says which interface the message is about. For PORT the Router Identifier is not needed and can be set to zero.

All multi-byte integers are sent in network byte order, most significant byte first.
sections.plainLanguage: If two roads connect the same two towns, you need names for the roads to say which one you mean. This gives each of the router's links its own name tag.

sections.title: The Interface Identifier Option
sections.content:
The option identifies the interface of a neighboring router through which a PIM Hello was sent. That lets PIM protocols refer to a particular interface on that neighbor.

A router needs to include the option only if it supports protocols that require it, though an implementation MAY always include it. How the identifier is used, and how unique and stable it must be, is left to the PIM protocols that use it. Such protocols should state their minimum requirements.

The identifier is 64 bits. The high 32 bits are the Router Identifier and the lower 32 bits are the Local Interface Identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The name tag has two parts: one part says which router, and the other says which doorway on that router.

sections.title: Rules for the Two Halves
sections.content:
The Local Interface Identifier must be unique among the router's PIM-enabled interfaces: there MUST NOT be two PIM interfaces with the same one. While an interface is up, its identifier MUST stay the same. If an interface goes down and comes up, the router SHOULD reuse it, but if the whole node restarts the identifiers MAY change. Many systems use an ifIndex (RFC 2863) for this. The value MUST be non-zero, because some protocols use 0 to mean that no interface is referenced.

The Router Identifier may uniquely identify the router, and how widely it must be unique depends on the protocols using it. An implementation picks it by a configured policy, for example an IPv4 unicast address of the router, but MUST allow it to be configured manually. It MAY reuse the identifier used by protocols such as BGP or OSPFv2 if the uniqueness needs are met. The value 0 means no Router Identifier is used, and an implementation MAY set it to zero if it only supports protocols that need uniqueness within one router.
sections.plainLanguage: No two doorways on one router may share a tag, and a doorway keeps its tag while it is open. A tag of zero means the tag is not being used.

sections.title: The Option Format
sections.content:
The option is a type-length-value element. The Type is 31 and the Length is 8, counting only the value part. The value holds the Router Identifier (4 bytes) followed by the Local Interface Identifier (4 bytes).

The Router Identifier field MAY be 0 when no protocol requires one, but it MUST contain either a valid Router Identifier or zero. The Local Interface Identifier is unique among all PIM-enabled interfaces on the router.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a small label with a type, a size, and then the two numbers that make up the name tag.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The identifier travels in PIM Hello messages, so the security considerations of RFC 4601 for Hello messages apply. In particular, a Hello may be forged and include an arbitrary Interface Identifier, or the identifier may be intentionally left out. The effects depend on how other protocols use the identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could write a fake name tag or remove a real one. How bad that is depends on what the neighbors do with the tags.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has assigned the value 31 to the Interface ID option in the PIM Hello options registry. No other registry action is described.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of Hello options now has this option written down as number 31.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the value part in bytes.

fields.name: Router Identifier
fields.desc: Identifies the router within some scope; 0 when not used.

fields.name: Local Interface Identifier
fields.desc: Unique among the router's PIM-enabled interfaces; non-zero.
